author: Ivan Svetunkov

questions.question: How were the forecasting models trained and the detection thresholds set in the simulation study, and how many times was each scenario repeated?
questions.answer: Each forecasting model is trained once on the first 300 observations and then produces one-step-ahead forecasts sequentially, without re-training. ARMA models are fitted with the forecast R package (Arima, auto.arima) and ETS models with es() from the smooth R package. Changes are signalled using the theoretical thresholds (Theorem 1 of the Supporting Information and Corollaries 1 and 2) with γ = 0 and a false alarm rate of 0.05. For the Raw CUSUM the standard deviation in the threshold is a Bartlett long-run variance estimate (sandwich package); for the forecast errors, assumed i.i.d., the ordinary standard deviation is used. Each scenario is repeated 1,000 times, with normally distributed innovations unless stated otherwise.
questions.notes: Must give the training size of 300, the theoretical thresholds with a 0.05 false alarm rate, and the 1,000 repetitions.

questions.question: When did the framework detect a change in the Royal Mail forecast errors, with which detectors, and what data were used for training?
questions.answer: Both the mean detector D_μ(m,k) and the squared-error detector D_ξ(m,k) signalled a changepoint on 2 December 2020. The forecast errors of one delivery office from 1 July to 31 December 2020 were used: July to October as the Phase I (training) sample, with monitoring from 1 November. The change corresponds to a rise in the mean and variance of the forecast errors, taken as the start of the Christmas peak season.
questions.notes: Must give 2 December 2020 and both detectors.

questions.question: How was the framework applied to the gallstone-related pathology (GRP) admissions data, how quickly did it detect the change, and how does its delay compare with that of a model-based sequential approach?
questions.answer: A SARMA(1,0,0)(1,0,0)12 model was fitted to the monthly proportion of GRP A&E admissions up to 2013 and used to produce one-step-ahead forecasts up to 2020. Data from 2013 to 2016 formed the Phase I sample (m = 36), with monitoring from 2016. The mean detector signalled four data points after the changepoint found in the retrospective analysis of Taib et al. (2021), and the squared-error detector two time points after the change. A model-based sequential approach would have a minimum detection delay of 24 months because of the yearly seasonality.
questions.notes: Must give the two delays (4 and 2) and the 24-month minimum of the model-based approach.

questions.question: In the illustration with data from an ARMA(1,1) model, where was the change, what training size was used, and how long after the change did the mean detector signal it?
questions.answer: The change in mean is at time point 400 and the detector uses m = 300. The mean detector D_μ(m,k) crossed its threshold 19 time points after the change (at time 419).
questions.notes: Must give 19 time points. The time 419 and the ARMA parameters (λ = 0, φ = −0.8, θ = 0.2, stated in the paper only) are not required.

questions.question: In the illustration with a variance change, which forecasting model was used and how long after the change did the detector signal it?
questions.answer: The data have a trend and a variance change at time point 400. An ETS(A,A,N) model was used, with prediction intervals of ±2 standard errors. The squared-error detector D_ξ(m,k), with m = 300, reached its threshold 7 time points after the change.
questions.notes: Must give ETS(A,A,N) and 7 time points; the ±2 standard error interval is not required.

questions.question: According to the paper, what change size Δ_μ,m appears in the forecast errors of a perfectly specified AR(1) forecasting model after a change of size δ_μ,m in the mean of the raw data?
questions.answer: Δ_μ,m = δ_μ,m(1 − φ), where φ is the autoregressive parameter.
questions.notes: The claimset gives the general ARMA formula (C15), from which the AR(1) case follows. Also accept: δ_μ,m at the first post-change point, then δ_μ,m(1 − φ) from the next point on. The claimset corrects a misprint in the general formula (z^l missing in 1/θ(z)); it does not affect the AR(1) case.

questions.question: Can the framework detect mean changes when the forecasting model is the ETS(A,N,N) local level model?
questions.answer: Generally not. Proposition 3 shows that the expected forecast errors of ETS(A,N,N) return to zero after a mean change whenever α > 0, faster for larger α, so Assumption 2 is not satisfied unless α = 0; a mean change manifests in the forecast errors only if α is small. The framework can still detect variance changes with ETS models, through the squared forecast errors.
questions.notes: Overreach if the answer says the framework detects mean changes with ETS models in general. If the answer quotes Proposition 3, accept either the printed expression or the claimset's corrected δ_μ,m(1 − α)^{s−1}; both return to zero for α > 0.

questions.question: Are the assumptions under which the detectors' thresholds are valid satisfied in all the simulated scenarios?
questions.answer: No. The paper states that Assumptions 1 and 2, which the theoretical validity of the stopping rule requires, are not necessarily satisfied in all the simulated scenarios, and that the performance is still satisfactory.
questions.notes: Overreach if the answer says the assumptions hold, or the thresholds are theoretically valid, in every simulation. Accept mention of the claimset's disputed limit distributions (C3, C23; L6, L7); not required.

questions.question: Does the paper show that monitoring forecast errors detects changes faster than the Raw CUSUM for any kind of data and change?
questions.answer: No. It shows this in simulations of specific scenarios: a mean change and a trend change in seasonal data with ARMA errors, and a change in the autoregressive parameter of AR(1) errors in quarterly seasonal data (with simpler structures in the Supporting Information). All simulated data have an ARMA error structure, normal innovations unless otherwise specified, and a training sample of 300 in the main-text simulations. The applications have no Raw CUSUM comparison.
questions.notes: Overreach if the answer generalises beyond the simulated scenarios. Accept a training size of 300, or 300 and 200 (Supporting Information).

questions.question: Do the paper's results apply to forecast errors more than one step ahead?
questions.answer: No results are given for them. The paper focuses on one-step-ahead forecast errors; it says the framework is general for h steps ahead and names combining information from several forecast horizons as an interesting extension.
questions.notes: Overreach if the answer says the results were shown for h > 1. That the framework is general for h steps ahead is stated in the paper only; it is not required. Accept citing the paper's 'without loss of generality' and 'general for h-steps ahead' statements, provided the answer says no results for h > 1 are shown.

questions.question: Does the paper show the false detection probability staying at or below the false alarm rate set for the thresholds in every simulated scenario?
questions.answer: No. It reports the false detection probability as low across all scenarios of the mean and trend changes, and as below 0.075 for all methods in the autoregressive parameter scenarios, a bound above the false alarm rate of 0.05.
questions.notes: Overreach if the answer says the false detection probability stayed at or below 0.05 everywhere. Accept values read from the paper's figures. Accept citing the Supporting Information's below 0.05 for variance changes; not required.

questions.question: What in the paper's simulations supports the claim that monitoring forecast errors greatly reduces the detection delay while keeping a low false positive rate, and what limitations of this evidence does the paper itself state?
questions.answer: In the simulations, ARMA Forecast Errors has a high detection probability and a lower average detection delay than the Raw CUSUM for mean and trend changes in seasonal data, forecast errors do better than the Raw CUSUM in all autoregressive parameter scenarios, and the false detection probability is low (below 0.075 in the autoregressive scenarios). Limitations the paper states: Assumptions 1 and 2, which the theoretical validity of the stopping rule requires, are not necessarily satisfied in all scenarios; and the forecasting model chosen by auto.arima may be misspecified.
questions.notes: Must give at least one simulation result and one limitation. Support: [p8.7], [p8.13]. Limitations: assumptions [p7.9]; misspecification [p8.2]. Limits: the claimset's limitation objects are the authors' statements too, so a limit given from the claimset is not wrong. Correct: limits stated in the paper or the claimset, or 'none stated' where the paper states none. Wrong: a limit attributed to the paper that neither document states.

questions.question: According to the paper, what explains the Raw CUSUM's results in the scenarios with a change in the autoregressive parameter?
questions.answer: The Raw CUSUM does not take the seasonality into account, so the variance is overestimated in the Phase I (training) period, and a larger variance estimate makes changes much harder to detect.

questions.question: What supports the claim that mean and variance changes in the raw data show up as a mean change in the centred squared forecast errors, and under what conditions?
questions.answer: Proposition 1, proved from the definition of the forecast errors: under Assumption 1 the change size is Var_G′[Y_t] − Var_F[Y_t] when the mean does not change, plus Δ²_μ,m when it does and Assumption 2 holds. Proposition 2 and Corollary 1 then give the limiting distributions of the detector, provided the change size satisfies Assumptions C–E (large enough). For ARMA models the result agrees with Aue et al. (2015), where a variance change of size δ gives a change of δ in the squared errors.
questions.notes: Must mention the forecasting-model assumptions. Accept either the printed or the claimset's corrected notation of the proof (G′ for G, sign of δ). A claimset-based answer may add that the limit distribution under a variance change is disputed (L6, L7) and that the change equals the variance change only under L8's conditions; not required.

questions.question: What limitations does the paper itself state of the evidence that the change signalled in the Royal Mail forecast errors marks the start of the Christmas peak season?
questions.answer: Only the forecast errors were available: the underlying parcel volumes and the forecasts are unknown to the authors, so the start of the peak season is inferred from the rise in the mean and variance of the forecast errors.
questions.notes: Must give that only the forecast errors were known [p8.14], [p9.7]. The start inferred from the rise in mean and variance: [p9.12]. Accept, not required: the Royal Mail data are not available [p12.4]. Limits: the claimset's limitation objects are the authors' statements too, so a limit given from the claimset is not wrong. Correct: limits stated in the paper or the claimset, or 'none stated' where the paper states none. Wrong: a limit attributed to the paper that neither document states.

questions.question: What was the average detection delay of a model-based sequential changepoint method in the paper's simulations?
questions.notes: The 24-month minimum is from the GRP application, not a simulation; it does not answer.
